Chapter 5 · pp. 75–97

Managing a Team

The Manager's Path, First Edition

Managing a team is more than managing its individuals: the job changes, and it is a new set of skills rather than a continuation of senior engineering. This chapter turns from people tasks back to the technical, strategic and leadership parts of running one team. It argues for staying a little in the code, gives a first-aid kit for dysfunctional teams (not shipping, people drama, overwork, collaboration problems), questions the manager-as-shield, and lays out how to drive good decisions with data, product sense and retrospectives. Conflict avoidance gets a list of dos and don'ts, toxic team members — the brilliant jerk, the noncommunicator, the person who lacks respect — get direct treatment, and the chapter closes with rules of thumb for planning a team's quarter (pp. 75–97).

From the book

Introduction

At every step beyond this one the job is different, and the hardest thing to prepare for is doing totally different things (p. 75). The author's job description for an engineering lead (pp. 75–76):

  • Spends less time coding, but still ships bug fixes and small features without blocking the team; mostly clears bottlenecks and roadblocks.
  • Identifies the highest-value projects and keeps the team focused on them, partnering with the product lead on scope.
  • Plans headcount and recruits.
  • Manages people with skills different from their own, with frequent feedback — not only at review time.
  • Leads the technical roadmap for the product group ("pillar"): timeline, scope and risk; identifies strategic technical debt, weighs its cost and benefit, and proposes when to pay it down.

Becoming a People Manager (bethanye Blount, pp. 76–77). Made a manager in a company that had resisted managers, she managed engineers far more senior than she was and couldn't lead by knowing the most. One helped with ongoing feedback; the other transferred away, then returned months later. Being a good manager isn't about having the most technical knowledge; supporting people mattered more.

From the book

Staying Technical

Engineering management is a technical discipline: even when you stop writing code you guide technical decisions, hold architects and senior staff accountable, and check decisions pass the "technical smell test" in the context of the team and business. Without technical credibility you face an uphill battle and limited options (p. 77).

Why write small code at this level (p. 78)?

  • You feel the bottlenecks. A slow build, long deploys or a nightmare on-call show up when an experienced engineer struggles with trivial tasks — imagine how your team feels. Technical debt is easier to spot and prioritize after slogging through the code.
  • You can judge what's possible. When the product manager has a crazy idea you can evaluate it (beware overconfidence), and find the shortest path through the systems.

Some companies split the tracks so cleanly that new managers get large teams at once and code only on nights and weekends. There, stay technical until you've mastered what you want to learn, then decide: stopping too early may cap you at middle management (p. 78).

From the book

Debugging Dysfunctional Teams: The Basics

Missed deliverables, unhappy people, quitting, a frustrated product manager, low energy — something is wrong, but what (p. 79)?

DysfunctionWhat's going onWhat to do (pp. 79–81)
Not shippingEven research teams have deliverables; humans feel good setting and meeting small goals. Infrequent releases (weekly or less) hide poor release tooling, manual testing, oversized features and developers who can't break work downBalance pushing and holding back; roll up your sleeves on the slipping part; remove the bottlenecks. The author's team went from painful hours-long weekly releases to daily ones — releases had been a point of resource contention, and morale improved immediately
People dramaThe "brilliant asshole" kept too long; or someone who stirs drama, dwells on the negative, gossips, plays us-against-themBe brave and act quickly. Your manager may find the brilliant jerk even harder to tackle, seeing only output; a team move may help. Give the negative person clear examples and quick corrective feedback — or help them leave on good terms
Unhappiness due to overworkUsually has fixable rootsIf production instability causes it, slow the roadmap and measure alerts, downtime and incidents; dedicate 20% of every planning session to "sustainability" work. In a time-critical crunch, be a cheerleader — help with the work, order dinner, promise a break — then learn from it: cut features, push back on unrealistic dates
Collaboration problemsFriction with product, design or other teams drags everyone downRegular touchbases with peers; gather actionable feedback; never undermine peers in front of your team. Within the team, create time together that isn't about work — even introverts want relatedness

Run it: Release cadence and contention simulates the same stream of changes shipped weekly and daily, and counts how often a broken change blocks everyone else's.

Ask the CTO: Managing a Former Peer (pp. 82–83). Acknowledge the awkwardness and ask for honest help; be a little vulnerable. Use your new power to override technical decisions very cautiously, and don't micromanage former peers, who are sensitive to you being "rewarded." Let go of old work — hand former peers control of technical areas you owned and give juniors new challenges; first-line managers write small features and fixes, not deep new systems. Pick your battles: they may even try to undermine you.

From the book

The Shield

The advice to be a shield — a "bullshit umbrella" — is half right (pp. 83–84):

Shielding helpsShielding hurts
Teams exposed to irrelevant toxic drama get distracted and stressed; engineering doesn't need customer-service politics. Help people focus on what they can changePeople need context, not just goals: if a system that isn't ready means operational problems in November, the team deserves to know — context is how they decide where to spend energy
Workplace drama is usually an ego-entertaining drainDenying outside events (layoffs elsewhere that the team hears about secondhand) creates the feeling something bad is being hidden. Share it plainly and with low emotion
You're a shield, not a parent. Treating the team as fragile children makes you take their mistakes and disagreements personally; they are adults owed respect

From the book

How to Drive Good Decisions

The product manager owns the roadmap and the tech lead the technical details, but you are accountable for the team's progress through both — judged on decisions you can only guide (p. 84).

PracticeHow (pp. 84–86)
Create a data-driven team cultureAdd team productivity (time to complete features) and quality data (time on outages, bugs found in QA or after release) to the business data your product head already uses
Flex your own product musclesWhoever depends on your work — external users, other engineers, a support team — is your customer. Customer empathy gives engineers context and shows where engineering effort matters most
Look into the futureThink two steps ahead: technical projects often win support by enabling features (rewriting checkout to add Apple Pay; a framework that streams changes over WebSockets). Ask product what's coming; follow technology
Review the outcome of decisions and projectsDid the team move faster after the rewrite? Did customers behave as predicted? What did the A/B tests teach?
Run retrospectivesRegularly, agile or not, on requirements, code quality and day-to-day — more subjective than metrics but arguably more valuable, because it is what the team itself notices

From the book

Good Manager, Bad Manager: Conflict Avoider, Conflict Tamer

Two overworked teams, each with a "Charles" on a pet project (pp. 86–87):

Jason, the conflict avoiderLydia, the conflict tamer
Asks the team to vote on which projects to drop; they vote out Charles's project — a surprise only to Charles, whom Jason never toldTells Charles in a 1-1 that priorities changed and the team needs him on the rewrite — an unpleasant conversation she owns
Never says no to other teams, never asks for more people; the team can't prioritize and nurses grudgesPushes for more people, explains why the team took the project, structures technical disagreements with options and feedback
Seen as cool but impossible to get decisions from; nobody feels secureSeen as tough but fair; the team gets through disagreements and collaborates well

Constant bickering is painful, but artificial harmony is worse: create a safe environment for disagreement rather than pretend it doesn't exist (p. 87).

The dos and don'ts of managing conflict (pp. 87–89):

Don'tDo
Rely exclusively on consensus or voting. It assumes impartiality, equal stakes and equal knowledge, which teams rarely have — and it can be cruel. Don't stage votes to deliver bad news you should deliver yourselfSet up clear processes to depersonalize decisions: shared goals, risks and questions; a named decision owner; who is consulted and who is informed
Turn a blind eye to simmering issues. Major problems shouldn't surface first in a review — or first through several peers' feedback, which means you weren't paying attentionAddress issues without courting drama. Is it ongoing? Have you seen it? Do many people struggle with it? Is there a power dynamic or bias? You're not the team's therapist
Take it out on other teams. Avoiders often turn bully toward outsiders after cross-team incidents, venting the accountability they won't demand at homeBe kind, not nice. Nice is polite-society smoothness; kind is telling someone they aren't ready for promotion, with what to do about it, or that their behaviour disrupts meetings
Be afraid — of deciding, seeming demanding, people quitting or disliking youGet curious about your motives: am I pushing this decision to the team because they're best placed, or because I fear an unpopular call?

From the book

Challenging Situations: Team Cohesion Destroyers

A test of a happy team — do they stay for evening pizza? — is flawed (obligations aren't disengagement), but gelled teams do joke, get coffee and feel friendly (pp. 89–90). The real goal is psychological safety: willingness to take risks and make mistakes in front of each other. Build it by getting to know people — the birthday party, the ski trip, the marathon training — which fosters relatedness. "Culture fit" can mask discrimination but comes from a wise place: friendly teams gel faster and do better (p. 90). Toxic people make everyone around them less effective, so deal with them quickly (p. 90).

TypeBehaviourWhat to do (pp. 90–92)
The brilliant jerkOutsized results, ego-driven; bullies with intellect, cuts down dissent, ignores those deemed unequal. Clings to brilliance like a life raftBest of all, don't hire one; firing takes rare confidence, but at least don't promote them. Expect a fight over all feedback. Openly refuse to tolerate bad behaviour — here criticism may be public, neutral and in the moment ("Please do not speak to people that way; it is disrespectful") — but only for behaviour harmful to the group. Priorities: protect the team, then each individual, then yourself
The noncommunicatorHides information, works in secret to unveil perfect work, reverts others' commits or does their tickets, avoids code and design reviewNip it in the bud, making clear it misses expectations. Look for the root: fear of being found lacking, wanting more responsibility, a harsh culture, or a team excluding someone different — then fix the team or move the person
The employee who lacks respectDoesn't respect you, or their teammatesAsk whether they want to be on your team. Yes — lay out expectations clearly and calmly. No — move them or help them leave. Pull off the Band-Aid: the rest of the team will wonder whether they're right

From the book

Advanced Project Management

The organization will expect off-the-cuff estimates and concrete plans: whether your team can take a project, how big it is, how many people you'd need (p. 93). You don't own the agile day-to-day; you own the accomplishments measured in months, not weeks (p. 93).

Rule of thumbDetail (pp. 93–95)
None of this replaces agileAgile planning smooths the day-to-day; the manager plans the larger picture
10 productive engineering weeks per engineer per quarterOf about 13 weeks, vacations, meetings, review season, outages and onboarding take the rest. Q1 tends to be most productive, Q4 least
Budget 20% for sustaining engineeringTesting, debugging, legacy cleanup, version migrations. It chips away at mid-size legacy code each quarter or absorbs delays; scheduling features to 100% slows features down
Near deadlines, it's your job to say noThe only way to hit a date is to cut scope: say no to engineers who want prerequisite work (hack now, or the right implementation?) and to product on must-haves, giving options and their costs
Double quick estimates; plan longer onesOff-the-cuff: guess and double it. For more than a couple of weeks, double it and say you need planning time — long tasks can take far more than twice the guess
Be selective about what you bring to the team to estimateYou absorb uncertainty. Don't be a telephone relaying every request — nor a black hole; set up a team process for new features and complaints

Ask the CTO: Joining a Small Team (pp. 95–96). As a new manager of five engineers with new code: get walked through the architecture, testing and release; do the developer onboarding; read code reviews; ship at least a couple of features in your first 60 days — pair, get reviewed, do a release, take a support rotation. Management onboarding goes slower, but you gain understanding and technical credibility.

From the book

Assessing Your Own Experience

Questions for reflection (pp. 96–97): what did you stop doing to make time for the new job? How well do you know the team's day-to-day pain? When did you last write a feature or pair? Who causes most of the negativity, and what's your plan? How does the team make decisions, and which do you own? When did you last review a finished project against its goals, or cut scope — and how did you choose?

Trade-offs at a glance

ChoiceBuysCosts
Manager keeps coding small thingsFeels bottlenecks; credibilityTime; must not block the team
Manager stops coding earlyTime for managementTechnical obsolescence; capped career
Weekly releasesFewer release eventsHidden pain, contention, broken last-minute changes
Daily releasesSmall batches; less contentionNeeds automation and tooling investment
Full shieldFocusNo context for decisions; rumours
Voting on decisionsLooks democraticUnequal knowledge and stakes; cruelty; avoided accountability
Depersonalized decision processFair, predictable decisionsSetup effort; a named owner must decide
Features at 100% of scheduleLooks productiveFeatures slow down; no buffer
20% sustaining workSystems stay easy to change; slackFewer features this quarter

Recap

Key takeaways

  • Stay technical enough to feel the bottlenecks. Small features and bug fixes reveal slow builds, painful deploys and on-call misery, and keep your judgement and credibility (pp. 77–78).
  • Debug the basic dysfunctions: teams that don't ship (often infrequent releases hiding pain), people drama, overwork (dedicate 20% of planning to sustainability), and collaboration problems (pp. 79–81).
  • Shield the team from drama, not from context. People need to know why goals exist; denying outside events breeds gossip; and you're not their parent (pp. 83–84).
  • You're accountable for decisions you only guide: bring data, flex product muscles, look two steps ahead, review outcomes, and run retrospectives (pp. 84–86).
  • Tame conflict instead of avoiding it. Don't hide behind votes; depersonalize decisions with clear processes; address issues early; be kind, not nice (pp. 86–89).
  • Toxic people destroy psychological safety. Openly refuse to tolerate the brilliant jerk's behaviour, address the noncommunicator's fear, and ask the disrespectful person whether they want to be on the team (pp. 89–92).
  • Plan with rules of thumb: about 10 productive weeks per engineer per quarter, 20% for sustaining work, say no near deadlines by cutting scope, double quick estimates, and shield the team from estimate requests (pp. 93–95).

Practice

Check yourself

Questions and answers are the vault's, written from the notes above; answers cite the book's printed pages.

1Why should an engineering lead still write small features and bug fixes?Show answer

To feel the bottlenecks — slow builds, painful deploys, bad on-call — and spot technical debt, and to judge what the systems can do when product proposes something (p. 78).

2How did moving from weekly to daily releases improve morale on the author's team?

pp. 79–80.

3What is wrong with being a total shield?Show answer

People need context for their goals to make good decisions; denying outside events breeds gossip; and shielding can slide into parenting adults (pp. 83–84).

4Why was Jason's team vote on Charles's project a mistake?Show answer

Voting assumes equal stakes and knowledge and can be cruel; he used it to avoid delivering bad news himself, and Charles had never been told (pp. 86–87).

5When is public criticism appropriate with a brilliant jerk?Show answer

When the behaviour visibly harms the team and you don't want the culture to mimic it — delivered neutrally and in the moment; behaviour that only undermines you personally belongs in private (p. 91).

6How many productive weeks per engineer should you plan for in a quarter, and how much sustaining work?

p. 94.

7What is the doubling rule, and when isn't it enough?Show answer

For off-the-cuff estimates, take your guess and double it; for projects longer than a couple of weeks, double it but insist on planning time, because long tasks can take far more than twice the guess (p. 95).

Supplement

Beyond the book

Vault supplement — not from the book.

  • Psychological safety is Amy Edmondson's term (Administrative Science Quarterly, 1999); Google's Project Aristotle study of its own teams (2015) found it the most important factor in team effectiveness.
  • Small batches. The book's release story matches a central finding of the DORA research (Forsgren, Humble and Kim, Accelerate, 2018): frequent deploys of small changes go with lower change failure rates. The lab is a toy model of why batch size matters, with invented failure rates.
  • RACI. "Who should be consulted and who needs to be informed" (p. 87) echoes the RACI matrix — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — used to assign decision ownership.

Run it

Release cadence and contention

Five engineers each merge one change a day for 120 working days. Each change has a 4% chance of breaking the release. A release ships every change merged since the last one; if the batch holds a broken change, the whole batch waits a day for each broken change to be found and fixed. The script compares weekly and daily releases: how many releases, how many were blocked, how big each batch was, and how long a change waited from merge to production.

cd books/the-managers-path/lab/05-release-cadence
python3 release_cadence.py
